en: Victorious is the Bhairava of Consciousness, worshipped on all sides by the sovereign goddesses of the senses with a continuous stream of the flowers of objects blossoming within the garden of his own self-reflection.

2. Victorious is the Lord of the Circle (*cakranātha*), whose own circle of powers consists of the mass of his own energies in the form of rays arising without desire, and who performs worship fashioned by Bhairava through the manifestation of the universe with his own Goddess, the power consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). 3. [He is] the severer of the obstruction caused by the sequence and non-sequence of ritual action.
I take refuge in the Divine Wheel, which has swallowed up Death (Kṛtānta) in its play;

for here [in this wheel] is the true reality of the Supreme Lord of the Wheel of Bhairava, in whom all the turmoil of mental constructs is gathered within the pinnacle of the cave that is the unsurpassed abode;

who is both the ineffable signifier and the signified, beyond description and yet the very vision itself; without beginning or end, both internal and external in form; and though neither the worshipped nor the worshipper, he is nevertheless the unfolding sequence of the descent of the primordial, emerging agency, through which the unartificial process of worship—the worshipper and the worshipped—is brought forth in the manner of the fivefold flow.

The method [of practice] that "shines forth" has been determined by the Lord himself in his own words in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava* and other such works— which follow the path of the unrefuted tradition of bliss and resonate with the inner essence of all the scriptures—
as well as in the *Śrīsvatantrabhaṭṭāraka* and others.
Q: By such statements as "without performing a mental sacrifice" (SvaTa 3.32c), the offering of all states of being—which exceeds the mental sacrifice—is intimated;
the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka-pāda, making that very offering manifest through the medium of a hymn, introduces it with the opening verse.
Oṃ! Homage to the one who steals away the body of Time through the web of the digits of the Sun;

homage to the pedestal that is both the support and the supported, to Bhava, the bestower of non-becoming. Vivṛti: Homage to Bhava, for whom the arising and ceasing of existence are manifested as mere play.

The word *namaḥ*—through the expansion of its two constituent syllables and by way of making known the entire nature of that [reality] as conveyed by the word ending in the dative case—indicates the state of *unmanī*; thus, it means: "I dissolve the mind therein."

He who "removes" (apaharati)—that is, whose nature it is to remove—either the body of time (*kāladeha*) or the desire for enjoyment (*kāmīha*) which manifests as the conceptualization of time, by means of the "net of solar digits" (*sūryakalājāla*), that is, the mass of rays consisting of twelve [suns]; this is indicated by the term "without succession" (*akrama*). He is so called because his nature is to remove the body of Great Time (*mahākāla*), which consists of the great ego (*mahāhaṅkāra*), by removing the body of time through the piercing of the central abode (*madhyamadhāma*) by means of the net of the digits of the Sun, which consists in transcending the plane of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvabhūmi*).
Thus it has been said:

Q: "Kālī, who completely devours Mahākāla," and so forth. Consequently, by means of the web of solar digits (*sūryakalājāla*) or indeed the web of solar digits itself, she seizes away the body of Time; thus, the great flood that completely devours is manifested.

For indeed, in the arising of the Mistress of the Wheel of Supreme Consciousness (*paracittacakreśvarī*), which is the Nameless (*anākhyā*) and beyond succession, no such thing as "Time" is logically possible.

This has been stated by me myself in the *Akramakallolakārikā*: "If time is to be consumed by time, by what would time itself be consumed? If time is not to be consumed at all, then why is it so [described] as being consumable?"
How could Death, having been swallowed by the throbbing inner Light, swallow [anything] again?
For, being non-throbbing, it lacks luminosity; or rather, is it not the case that it cannot be grasped internally?
Likewise, the support and the supported—the six paths and that which transcends them, existence and non-existence—belong to this [Light] precisely because they abide within it.

Because he is joined with exertion (*udyoga*), illumination (*avabhāsa*), relishing (*carvaṇa*), dissolution (*vilāpana*), and the subsequent duties (*taduttarakṛtya*), he is like a pedestal (*pīṭha*); thus, [the name] belongs to him whose pedestal is such. However, according to the reading *ādhārādhyeyapīṭhāya*, Śakti herself is the object of meditation (*dhyeyā*) upon the support (*ādhāra*); because she possesses a foundation through her presiding over that [support], he is the one whose pedestal is such—to that Bhava, who brings about non-becoming (*abhavadāyin*), who destroys the inauspicious (*aśivaparikhaṇḍana*), or who bestows liberation (*mokṣaprada*), salutation! By this, through the presentation of the state of being the pedestal of the support and the supported—which removes time and body—the [salutation] characterized by the constant realization of all things as one's own self (*sarvātmasātkaraṇa*) is eternally arisen.
This method of artificial worship has been set forth;
here, by the word *apahāri*, the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is expressed, and by the word *pīṭha*, the sequence of maintenance (*sthitikrama*).
With the word "existence" (bhava), emission (sṛṣṭi) is indicated; thus, this verse, concluding with emission, has discussed the "stream of the non-sequential" (akramaugha).
Because the fourth [category] serves as the foundation for all sequential and non-sequential [categories], it is not mentioned separately.
Now, by means of the rhythmic movement of maintenance, emanation, and withdrawal as the primary focus, he demonstrates the second sequence of worship:
Homage to Śiva, whose body is supreme bliss, whose form is unmanifest, who wears the digits of the moon— the beloved of the young night— as his lotus garland.

Vivṛti: "To Śiva"—to Him whose form (*mūrti*) is unmanifest (*avyakta*), being unrevealed as a distinct protrusion due to the predominance of the states of non-existence, existence, and stability; to Him who possesses a nature that does not falter even amidst great immersion (*āveśa*). Thus it has been explained. By virtue of His childhood and so forth, this "digit" (*kalā*) of the Beloved of Night—the Lover of the Night of Time (*kālarātri*), the Supreme Bhairava—which exists through the nature of differentiation, is itself cherished by the petals of the eight groups (*varga*) endowed with the three veils (*āvaraṇa*) of Aghora, Ghora, and Aghorātighora.
She herself is the lotus for that garland, the support for that which is supported, or [the support] for that which is contained therein;
she is the digit of the beloved of Night, the Goddess of Withdrawal—
and so too says our son.
Q: "Ever seated upon the head of the throne of Śiva, free from the process of the measurement of time and its parts;
by her very slenderness, she transcends all notions of thinness—victorious is that certain partless digit (kalā) beyond all sequence.
Thus it is said in the *Vājasaneyabhaṭṭārikā*.
Q: The Avadhūtī is beyond conventional conduct and dwells within all beings;
she plays with states consisting of the Self, just as a child plays with toys.
Having divided oneself by means of the self into the awakened and the full states,
one should intensely cultivate them for the sake of play, through both the unawakened and the awakened.
Thus: "to Mālinī" and "to the Sustainer" constitute the state of maintenance (*sthiti*). "To the one whose body is bliss" constitutes emission (*sṛṣṭi*), because that [state] has the nature of bliss;
"to the one of unmanifest form" constitutes withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
This sequence of worship is also eternally established.

Now he promises the worship according to the sequence of the third wheel, whose nature consists of the subordinate processes of emanation and maintenance: Homage to Hara, the Supreme Self, who resides within the womb of the interior of mantra, and who effects the striking together, dissolution, and separation of the flood of bonds.

Viv: Regarding "of the nooses"—the flood (*ogha*) of impurities consisting of the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* [impurities], their "clashing" (*saṃghaṭṭa*) is an emergence by some causeless process;
through that, or in that, or of that, there is this dissolution (*laya*).

Likewise, there is separation (*viśleṣa*), which is a state of distinctness. Because it exists as having the nature of performing that [dissolution and separation], its inherent capacity for concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) is implied, since it always performs these three functions.

Regarding the phrase *mantragarbhodarasthāya*, there is a threefold tradition of the Guru: [the first interpretation is that] "she whose womb contains the mantras" is Mālinī; he who dwells within her womb—that is, internally as the signified (*vācya*)—is thus [described].

Alternatively, "mantragarbha" means the womb of the mantras, which is the first vowel; its "belly" (udara) is the middle digit (*madhyamakalā*), consisting of half a *tuṭi*, which abides there by rejecting the subsequent position. Alternatively, because it possesses the nature of protecting through contemplation (*manana-trāṇa-dharmitva*), it is called "mantra" when rays (*marīci*) abide and arise; thus, this very "non-noise-noise" (*anārāvarāva*), by way of being a convergence of sounds (*rāva-saṃghaṭṭaka*), [is the one who]—O Bhairavī, you who are unborn (*ajā*), who cause the melting away of the five causes that have not been performed, and whose abode is most formidable! [Note: The provided text fragment ends with a sandhi-conjunction (*Q: tvām ajām...*). The translation reflects the grammatical structure and the intended philosophical meaning of the passage.]

Q: He is so described because he abides within the womb—that profound, cavernous form—of that [reality] whose nature is stated in our own *Akulakaulikātriṃśikā*, beginning with the verse: "I am struck with wonder at the violent friction of heroes produced by the expansive resonance resulting from the transgression of the Unstruck (*anāhata*) and the Struck (*hata*)," and so forth;
for in all these matters, the instruction of the Primordial Lord alone shines forth, since he alone is the Supreme Self.

For this very reason, by means of the words *bhava*, *śiva*, and *hara* in these three verses, it is indicated that the final *anākhyā* (the Unnameable), which follows the instruction on emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest, pervades the end of all things because it is beyond the range of speech. Here, by the two words *ogha* and *saṃghaṭṭa*, emanation and maintenance (*sthiti*) are illuminated, and by the word *hara*, withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); thus, an unfabricated form of worship is indeed described. 3.
Thus, since worship consisting of one’s own essential nature— which is uninterrupted, eternally established, without material substratum, infinite, and ever-increasing— is possible,

yet it is impossible to worship Śambhu— whether he be considered devoid of qualities or possessed of infinite qualities— by means of endless external, physical, verbal, or mental offerings, [the author], raising the doubt as to what this so-called "offering of internal disposition" (bhāvopahāra) might be, says:

CakBhst_4ab: Although you transcend all qualities and are beyond the range of even the Lord of Speech, CakBhst_4cd: nevertheless, my speech is ever intent upon praising you from the very depths of my heart. CakBhst_5ab: O You whose face is everywhere, I am rendered helpless by the overwhelming force of the sentiment of supreme devotion.
"O Lord, since I am impelled by You, there is no fault in me anywhere.

By the words *yadyapi* ("even though") and *tathāpi* ("nevertheless," "still"), which reveal a logical possibility even where none exists, it is stated that non-possibility itself is the ultimate possibility;

for indeed, although He transcends all attributes (*guṇātīta*), He nevertheless occupies the abode of the object of experience as a manifestation on the level of the finite world, by means of some principle that accomplishes the impossible, through His own nature as the object of experience.
Thus it was said by the Lord who awakens the ascetics:
"Whatever form I perceive as being higher, each of those is inferior to You;
yet there is no perception whatsoever that does not abide entirely within You."

From the heart up to the supreme abode, although You are eternally arisen in the form of Ādirūpa, it is by You alone— by this very primordial Lord (Ādibhaṭṭāraka)— that [the power] spreads forth when impelled with intensity through the nature of Vaikharī;
thus, I have no fault whatsoever, for I am arisen as one who is entirely absorbed in that [divine state],
were I indeed some other person.
There might indeed be an offense;
however, even if there were an offense, both I and you are one and the same reality,
and therefore, what could be the meaning of the word "offense"?

Thus it was said by me myself in the *Śivarava-stotra*: "Or rather, my mind proceeds toward praise, having been approved by [the Lord] who resides in the ether of the heart, whose form is devoid of birth and death, and who wears a crown as pure as the moon."

He by whom that state of non-differentiation from the aesthetic flavor (*bhakti-rasa*) has been transcended— such is this immersion (*āveśa*), which is the arising of an identity with everything in all directions;

by means of that, he is "helpless" (*vivaśa*) yet "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*), like an elephant under control, because his faces are turned everywhere toward the universe due to being reeling with the intoxication of the constant removal of veils through the chewing of the essence of his own awakened consciousness.
By this, the following is meant: there is no object of speech or action whatsoever that does not shine forth through its beautiful form as an object of your relish.

And thus, even by means of sleep-talking, insults, and the like, you alone are being praised; so he says, "viśvatomukhaḥ" (facing all directions), meaning either that whose face is from every side, or that whose face is everywhere.
The sense is that his manifestation extends unimpeded down to the forms of cattle, chickens, and so forth.
Thus it has been established that, in every respect, [the Self] is a single mass of consciousness that has neither risen nor set, and is immeasurable. //4–5//
O Śrīkaṇṭha, accept from me this unartificial worship of the inner state (bhāvapūjā), offered by one who is adorned with the ashes of the cremation ground purified by the dust of your lotus feet.
Viv: *Śrī* is the address of Him whose throat—the abode of non-differentiation—is the power (*śakti*) that brings about the splendor of the manifold variety of the universe.

The word "accept" (*gṛhāṇa*), used in the sense of a request, indicates that it is You alone who manifest as both the recipient and the object to be given; this is suggested by the word *akṛt-kṛtrima*.

Your feet are the four states, such as *piṇḍastha* and so forth; these themselves are the lotus (*abja*). Within that [lotus] is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and its effects, which take the form of mental constructs (*vikalpa*) brought forth by those [feet].

Because it colors, it is *rajas*; by that [quality], or rather, purified by it, the accumulated splendor (*citābhūti*)—which, through the winnowing of sound reasoning, has been exhausted, and which consists of the consciousness of universal dissolution or the form of universal manifestation—is present.

Having dwelt upon that distinguished ground, you, from me—who am about to proclaim [the teaching]—shall likewise, full of your own bliss, offer the worship of your inner being (*bhāvapūjā*) to me. //6//
He introduces that very [practice] by means of the sequence of bathing:
"Having bathed within the sacred ford known as the Lotus of the Heart, which is frequented by yogis,
and having washed my garments with full awakening, I worship the Dark-throated One."
Vivṛti: The "lotus of the heart" (*hṛtpuṣkara*) is the heart-lotus; having bathed there by fixing one's attention upon it, one effects the removal of all impurities.
Alternatively, it is called *hṛt* because it "takes away" (*harati*), being the form that withdraws [all things] into dissolution (*saṃhāra*).
This very lotus of the heart is the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), for therein one attains supreme rest among all the cakras.

In this context, taking up total purity, the yogins here consist of the supreme rays; perfect awakening is *saṃbodha*, which is itself the washed garment—pure at all times—which exists as the covering of everything without exception.
Thus, there is an expression of being both transcendent of all and consisting of all.

Śyāmakaṇṭha means one whose neck or throat is dark blue; he whose throat possesses the nature of a dwelling place that gathers together all forms within the great darkness of the whirlpool (ghaṭṭaka). As it is said:

"I salute Śiva, who is firmly embraced by Śivā—who has enjoyed the entire universe as her food, drink, and ornament—and who is impetuous in the festival of cosmic dissolution. (Utpaladeva, *Stotrāvalī* 16.19–21)
Thus [ends the seventh section].
Regarding the vessel for the *argha* offering, he says:
"The *argha* vessel is made from the abundant blood produced by living beings,
O you who possess the trunk of a skeleton-like body, Great Kāla."

Viv: Within the pervasive Lord, the abode of Bhairava, all beings—consisting of the five elements such as earth and so forth, which are manifestations of the fivefold power—are woven and interwoven. The blood produced therein consists of the essence of consciousness (*cid-rasa*) arising from the dissolution of their own material forms. With these, the vessel for the *argha* offering—the receptacle for worship consisting of great reflective awareness (*mahā-vimarśa*)—is formed; it is the very form of the dissolution within the oyster-shell of the single Power (*eka-śakti*). This applies to all.

It is performed within the center of the abode of Kalāsaṃkarṣiṇī, inside the skull-bowl of the corpse-like body of Great Time (Mahākāla), which has been split open by ascending to the stage of non-conceptuality (*avikalpabhūmi*);
enough with this disclosure of the secret. //8//
Whatever web of conceptual constructions there is for the apprehension of external objects, each of those is a family of gatekeepers to be worshiped by the wise;

for the "gate" (dvāra) is characterized as the state of mind transcending the mind (*manonmanā*) because it projects external objects, and the "family" (*kula*) residing therein is the family of the gatekeepers— the assembly of those who stand at the gate.

For it is the very flavors of mental constructs that, by flowing through immersion in the flavor of one's own essential nature (svarūpa), cast [the object] into external receptacles when not yet shared;
and thereafter, being thus honored, they deliver it into the presence of the King who is one's own essential nature.
Thus, with their minds surrendered to the worshipful One, they attend to the portions of their own power. //9//

O Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain, you are worshipped during the eclipses of the moon and the sun within the secret mandala of deep sleep, which is liberated from all obscurations without exception.

Viv: Because of its "moving" (*camana*), as it vibrates (*cimicimāyamāna*) precisely within [the body] rather than being external; and because of its "flowing" (*dravana*), as it spreads outward in the form of the worldly course of life;
and likewise, because of its "well-filling" (*su-ūraṇa*), the words *candra* (moon) and *sūrya* (sun) include both the waking and dreaming states.
When there is the grasping— that is, the making one's own— of those two,

[the individual soul and the intellect], then, being liberated from all veils (aśeṣāvaraṇaiḥ), that is, from all limiting adjuncts (sarvopādhibhiḥ), [one abides] in that fourth state (turīye dhāmni) wherein the sphere of deep sleep (sauṣupta-maṇḍala) is concealed (gupta), meaning hidden (tirohita).

Born of the mountain, you are the power (*śakti*) shining forth from the immovable and eternal abode; O Beloved, whose own abode rests within her, you are constantly worshipped and experienced through this invocation. 10.
O Lord of the Three Worlds, the seat is that which is free from the delusions of loss, gain, arising, effort, existence, and non-existence, and is established in pure cognition alone;

for it is liberated from the conceptual constructions of abandonment, grasping, emergence, action, being, and non-being, precisely because it transcends the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

The mere act of valid cognition (*pramiti*), which is in itself the fruit and devoid of distinction, is the "seat" (*āsana*) by way of being its defining characteristic, since even that [cognition] is dependent [on something else]. For you, who have transcended even that and are indefinable (*avyapadeśya*),
it is "reported" (*nivedyate*)— in the reading *nivedyate*, it is known completely (*niḥśeṣeṇa vedya*), experienced as being of that very nature.

The seat (āsana) is indicated as being independent of the six categories of objects—such as rejection, acceptance, and so forth—for it is the presiding ground of the three worlds characterized by the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. //11//

O Lord of the World, I bestow the gift of the Form, augmented by the radiance of the power of non-manifestation, which is established upon the Fourth Seat. "Augmented" (*upabṛṃhitam*) means "the act of augmenting" (*upabṛṃhaṇam*).

I bestow— that is, I contemplate— the manifestation of the power whose essence is uninterrupted wonder, which is devoid of the appearance of external objects; it is the granting of the delineation of fullness to the form [of consciousness] which, though its true nature is concentrated, possesses a slight state of swelling.
And by means of the fullness of the I-consciousness, one is established in the Supreme.
(12) For one whose mind is free from the stain of the conceptualization of direction, time, and space, what wise person would perform the invocation and dismissal of the Lord Śiva? (13)

Vivaraṇa: For the Immovable One—whose body is the all-pervading pure consciousness that does not move—there is no conceptualization of separate directions, locations, or times; therefore, who that has realized the truth would perform the commencement of invocation or the rite of dismissal? For it is only when there is the possibility of distinct space and time that the bringing of someone from somewhere or the sending away of someone to somewhere could be conceived.
But here, since everything consists of that very [reality], whose is the invocation and from where is the invocation;
whose is the dismissal and where is the dismissal? Thus, by means of its total immersion alone, the attachment to all things is said to be transcended. //13//

Having churned the ocean of power with the two eyes of the sun and the moon, I offer to Śiva the anointing with the essence of supreme nectar. Vivṛti: That by which the unmanifest is anointed—that is, brought to manifestation—is the "anointing" (*abhaṅga*), the lubricant, which illuminates the sequence of emanation.
The two eyes are also [the subject] in the first sūtra. //14//

Cakrabhūti 15ab: Regarding the sense faculties and the objects of the senses that follow after passion and greed, [you possess] freedom from attachment and mastery; yours is the dry and cleansing anointing.
Vivaraṇa: Regarding the objects of the senses—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which have become the spheres of experience...
"In the case of the sense-faculties following after passion and greed" refers to two locative cases in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

"Freedom from attachment" (*niḥsnehatva*) and "sovereignty" (*prabhutva*) are utterly inconsistent; [the latter] is non-attachment, or rather, its manifestation as their presiding controller. [Objection: Like a Buddha, one would be full of all passions, or else like Bhairava, full of all hatred.
By this principle, the rubbing away [of impurities] is the uprooting of all latent impressions (vāsanās). //15//

Having quickly purified the bindu-tīrtha by means of the translucent *kalā*—which consists of the first letter (*a*) and takes the form of the head-goad (*aṅkuśa*), being the beginning of the collection of *kalās* in the form of the sixteen vowels—one should offer the bath of the nectar of its cessation (*virāma-rasa*) to Him whose crest is the half-moon. [Vivṛti: To Him whose crest is the *kalā* of the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), etc., by means of the translucent *kalā* which has the form of the first letter and the form of the head-goad, one should [purify] the bindu-tīrtha, which is of the nature of the hollow of both voids.

Having thoroughly purified [the body] and effected the binding of the *nirgranthi*, one should perform the consecration with the essence characterized by supreme satisfaction, which flows from the end of the soundless [state] through the process of cessation. //16//
Having cast down the transformations of your consciousness, we sport by rubbing the garments that blossom expansively in the sky of our own awakening. Vivaraṇa:

"One's own awakening" (*svaprabodha*) is indeed one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*); it is the "sky" (*ambara*) because it is unobstructed, and for that very reason, it is "expansive" (*udāra*), meaning magnificent.

Having performed the rubbing with that "garment"— which, expanding through its nature as the self of all, spreads forth by concealing the manifest effects— by means of a method of reversal and applying one's own attention,
when great *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium) is attained.
Once the grand displays of the great terror arising from duality have dissolved, let us cast in every direction the offerings of our own unimpeded self-awareness, free from all envy. //17//
CakBhst_18ab: Flowing forth like a mountain torrent from the abandonment of both cognition and the cognizable;
CakBhst_18cd: This stainless water for my feet, which bestows supreme bliss within, belongs to You.
Viv: Because both [cognition and the cognizable] are interdependent and thus lack an established nature as either insentient or sentient throughout the three periods of time.

Because there is no existence apart from consciousness (*cit*), it is immovable and thus a mountain (*naga*). From that mountain—which is of such a nature that it is free from the "cascade" (*jhara*) that has emerged, namely time (*kāla*) in the form of the decay of age (*vayahāni*)—there proceeds the water for the feet (*pādya*), which consists of supreme wonder (*paracamatkāra*).
[The root *jhṝṣ* means "decay of age."]
Thus, its form is *jhara*. [Question: By which rule is this derived? [Answer: From Pāṇini 3.3.57: *ṛdorap* ("The suffix *ap* is added after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*").

O All-pervasive Lord, receive this rinsing-water (*ācamana*) consisting of the flowing water of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) from the cave-sanctuary of the vibration that is the outflow of intense bliss.

[This refers to] that form of universal vibration which exists within the outflows of the vibrations beginning with the *guṇas*, and which manifests the modes of emission (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*prakāra*) through the simultaneous unfolding of closing and opening.

From the cavern of that very temple of vibration— a dwelling which, though characterized by slight swelling and a degree of movement, possesses an outpouring of intense and uninterrupted bliss because it is the first abode of all, such that there flows forth the wonder of the manifestation "I am"—
from that profound and deep abode, [arises...]
"Accept the rinsing-water (ācamana) whose essence is the form of non-duality as it unfolds; likewise, withdraw even the essence of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Thus, a certain method (naya) that transcends both bondage and liberation has been revealed.
Alternatively, there is the reading "from the cave of Mandara. //19//
Having washed the five-knot pearl necklace with the waters of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), I offer this priceless oblation (*argha*) at the feet [of the Lord], O Vṛṣākapi. (Viv:
O Vṛṣa, you who are intent on raining down the nectar of your own power.)
Likewise, O unshaken one, O you who are unwavering and immovable:
the pentad of knots characterized by Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and Ūrdhvagā;

the concentrations (dhāraṇās) such as Vāruṇī and the rest, which consist of binding the region through the knotting of the mind—these indeed are the waters. By means of these, through the process of leaping over the stages of attainment in the principal tradition numbering one hundred and eight, [one proceeds].
Having attained purity,
O Lord of the Mountain, you are worshipped with the flowers of praise consisting of three words, which are filled with the fragrance of consciousness blossoming in the garden of the Fourth state.
O Lord, Master of speech regarding the mountains!

With flowers in the form of hymns, which are filled with that fragrance of consciousness—the scent of awakening—that blossoms in the garden of the Fourth State (turīya), the forest of the nature of Parā; VIV: [I offer this].
You are worshipped with three forms of speech.

Among these, first, the praise belonging to the *paśyantī* level consists of the supreme state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the internal manifestation of "this-ness" and "I-ness," which are not distinct from its own essential nature.

Furthermore, even for the *madhyamā* level, your bouquet of praises consists of the unimpaired self-manifestation, whose ultimate intent is the non-trifling radiance that is free from the conceptual construction of subject and object.

However, although *vaikharī* speech possesses a clamorous quality and a readiness to manifest clearly such things as jars and cloths, because it lacks any other denotable object that exceeds the form of the Supreme Lord renowned in all directions, it is said that it is always characterized by the very merit of [pointing toward] Him; its purpose culminates in the thorough shattering of the determination of limited names.
O Consort of the Mountain-Born, your incense, possessing a luster like that of a burning wick, shines forth after piercing the aperture of Brahma with the weapon of the flame of the vital fire.
[Vivaraṇa: This flame of the fire, which is ignited by the vital breath—that is, the pinnacle of the fiery abode—...
It is called *astra* because it protects (*trāyate*) from below (*astāt*); or else, Niṣkalanātha is here aroused (*udvṛtta*),
and by that very [force] ignited by the falling of the *hikkā*, through the process of piercing the knots (*granthi*), there occurs the piercing of the *brahmagranthi*.

In this context, *prāṇa* is the weapon (*astra*) in the form of the flame of the fire-syllable *ha*, and so forth; it is called *dhūpa* because it fumigates the entire range of objects of knowledge and perfumes everything through its own vibration. //22//

The unstruck [sound] (*anāhatā*) which resounds within as the supreme Cow (*gauḥ*) in the highest abode—that bell, pregnant with the meaning of the text, is sounded before Śambhu. Vivaraṇa: It is called *aghaṇṭā* because it shatters (*troṭayati*) what is not a bell (*aghaṇṭa*). The supreme (*parā*) and most excellent (*prakṛṣṭā*) [bell] is pregnant with the meaning of the text—that is, all the categories of the signified and the signifier have been internalized. //23//
O Blessed One, for the sake of dispelling the darkness of delusion, I kindle the crest of the power (śakti) blazing from the fire at the root (kanda), which resembles the flame of a lamp. Vivaraṇa:
From the fire at the root—that is, from the abode in the center of the foundation—the crest of the power, in the form of the bindu, blazes forth.
I kindle that [power], which is of the nature of a lamp through the expansion of Śakti, by means of entering the mudrā whose crest is the needle of sound (nāda). //24//

The moon, which is the digit of nectar consisting of the abandonment of the mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), belongs to the one who wears the moon as a crown; may it serve as the perfect ointment for the liberation of those seeking release.

"Perfect ointment" (*samālambhana*) refers to the correct application [of consciousness] that consists of the dense essence of unperishing awareness, which remains after the abandonment of the fluctuations of cognition (*pramāṇa*), misconception (*viparyaya*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory (*smṛti*), and which sustains them.
Or, it may be a "complete immersion" (*samālambhaka*) because of the total pervasion [of all things]; for it is precisely such seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who are liberated.
Thus it was said by the venerable Utpaladeva:
"O Lord, he who perceives this entire sphere of objects as non-conceptual, [perceives] everything as Your very body."
Q: "When the world is completely filled by the side of one's own self, how could there be fear for this eternally blissful one?

(CakBhst 26ab). O Rudra, may that abode which has arisen from the power of *nāda*, which is free from the three impurities (*mala*), and which has cast open the bolt of the sky—may that *uṣṇīṣa* be yours! (CakBhst 26cd).
Viv: The *dhāman* (abode) is that which has arisen from the power of *nāda*, the digit situated above the *bindu*; it is designated as the splendor of *nādānta* because of its luminosity.

That very [abode] is devoid of the three impurities (*mala*), beginning with the *āṇava*, which are the causes of limitation; likewise, it has shattered the bolt of the sky and destroyed the wheel of knots that obstructs penetration into the supreme ether (*paravyoman*).
"Uṣaṇe" means "in the burning away of conceptual construction," and "uṣṇīṣam" refers to the Lord; this is also an etymological derivation based on the similarity of syllables.
May the stainless lotus of Brahman, blossoming upon the crest of you whose heart-ocean has been inundated by the nectar-shower of devotion to Bhava, be your crown-ornament.

Vivaraṇa: It is called the "crest-ornament" (*śekhara*) because it shines at the very tip and limit of the crown, being the lotus of Brahman that appears within the ocean of the heart made unfathomable by the rain of the nectar of devotion, which is the nature of the power of grace. (27)
The multitude of lotuses of awakening is your necklace of pearls;
the digit of the moon is your portion that is eternally risen and pervades the interior. Vivṛti:

For you who possess the necklace of pearls consisting of the offerings of sensory objects presented by the Mistress of the various forms and instruments, the very pervasion of the great space attained through union with Her is the "digit of the moon" (*candrakalā*), because it follows the meaning of the verbal roots *hlād* (to delight) and *dīp* (to shine).
Thus, the secret method of the Guru’s mouth, which causes the moon and the lotus to close, has been kindled. //29//
"O Lord of the World, having drawn forth from the lotus in the universal space by means of the solar rays of power (*śakti*), taste the flowing nectar of the moon of consciousness. Vivṛti:
"From the lotus in the universal space" means by way of the technique of the overflowing essence (*plāvakarasayukti*) through the process of the complete melting away [of all things].

Thus it was said by me in the *Cakreśvarabhairavāṣṭaka*: "We bow to that Śaiva sky wherein even the void, whose body is expanded by swallowing the four elements, though fiercely vast, is reduced to the size of an atom."

Thus, by the powerful rays of the sun [of consciousness], by the radiance of Mahākāla-Saṃkarṣiṇī, and by the chewing of the nectar-essence of the moon of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), there occurs the piercing of even the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhas*).

Following this, through the shattering of all abodes, there arises the manifestation of the beauty of the supreme vibration—the unsurpassed *paraparispanda*—which consists of the great expansion of the wheel that transcends all wheels (*cakrāticakrottaramahāsphāra*) and which dispels [all things] with a roar that devours both the terrible and the non-terrible (*ghorāghoraghasmara*). By this, a certain tradition (*saṃpradāya*), permeated by the latent impressions of the new moon (*amāvasyāvāsanā*), has been delineated. //29//
Having placed the mantra in the mind, that [mind] in its power, and that [power] in one's own ever-risen abode,
one should properly perform the rite of recitation and offer it to Śiva.
According to the principle that "a thousand [recitations] are mental," the mantra takes the form of the Lord Akula, who is perpetually uttered in the unstruck (anāhata) state.
Q: Even cowherds, women, children, and barbarians who speak vernacular tongues, and even creatures moving within the water, constantly utter that [mantra].

Thus, the fruit of all recitation is fulfilled, as it is filled by the complete cycle of lunar days (*tithi*), equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and solstices (*ayana*) situated within the minute subdivisions of the parts of the *kalā* whose essence is breath.

Having placed within the mind— which consists of concentrated attention— the manifestation of emanation and withdrawal, shown by the circumambulation of Mount Meru through the vibration of ritual actions from beginning to end, as the rosary beads are spread out by a single utterance;
and having placed even that mind, which has attained identity with the mantra, into the Śakti, which is the primordial power of expansion;

Even Śakti, within her own majesty—which is the supreme arising (*mahodaya*) characterized by the non-abandonment of both immanence (*sārvātmya*) and transcendence (*sarvottīrṇatā*)—attains her essential nature through the vitalization of the respective forms of all phonemes as they manifest according to the sequence of powers (*śaktikrama*).
Thus it has been said:
"Having ascended that power, the mantras [attain their strength]."
Thus, having accomplished such recitation through its performance or non-performance, one should properly and completely direct the intellect toward Śiva, one's own Great Lord, for His sake alone.

Beyond this constant engagement in recitation— which consists of the expansion of great heroic power and the state of essential identity (sāmarasya)— the recitation of bound souls (paśus) is merely brought about by phonemes that perish as soon as they are uttered.

It is thus stated that even from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is a seed devoid of potency, it does not attain the status of being a means for achieving perfect accomplishment. //30//
O Dhūrjaṭi, when all objects are either completely abandoned or grasped from the immeasurable light, I bind the mudrā of supreme pervasion, which is stainless. Viv: It shakes off everything.
He rushes everywhere,
he generates everything, and he pervades everywhere; thus, Dhūrjaṭi is the one whose meaning consists of the fourfold movement as it was proclaimed.
I bind— that is, I take as my own— this single mudrā of dissolution and emergence, which vibrates in five ways according to the method to be described;
for it is of unbounded majesty due to its infallibility in either the abandonment or the acceptance of all objects,
and it remains unstained by the temporal distinctions between the known, the knower, and time.
She consists of an unartificial, great pervasiveness.

It is she alone who, through the internal focus and external gaze, is Bhairavī by means of abandonment and grasping; and she is Lelihānā, whose form transcends abandonment and grasping through the throbbing wonder of the savoring of all things.
By the complete exhaustion of everything, even when only her own remainder remains, she is the *ekakaṅkiṇī*, whose nature consists of both relinquishing and grasping;
even when her own form is incapable [of further action], she is the *krodhinī*, whose essence is a throbbing greed to swallow that [remainder] and who is of that very nature;

and because she moves in the void (*kha*) solely through the cessation of the unfolding [of manifestation] consisting of the desire to expand and the desire to withdraw within the supreme void (*paravyoman*), she is the *khecarī*.

Thus, by virtue of being characterized by these very definitions, this single fivefold wisdom, as it unfolds, is savored through all the various seals (*mudrā*) and through the diverse distinctions of their respective expressions. //31//
CakBhst_32ab: Having blocked the two ears with the palms of the hands, whatever sound expands therein;
CakBhst_32cd: that is song, and then your instrumental music arises from the striking of the initial pair [of hands].
Viv: That which, sounding as if within the two cavities of the ears, is of a general nature—
He himself is the song;

by the contraction of both sides of the primordial bulb (ādyakanda), wandering through the forest of the flute-like various channels (nāḍī), he assumes the state of instrumental music, characterized by the most resonant distinctions of high notes produced from the unfolding of the sprouts of the various divisions of the *kalās*— namely, the dense (*ghana*), the hollow (*suṣira*), the sharp (*tāra*), the low (*mandra*), and the middle (*madhyama*)— and spread over by the rhythmic patterns (*prastāra*) of the dancing hands beginning with the five-fingered *caṣapuṭa*.
Or there is the reading "between the ear and the concha" (*śaṣkulīkarṇayor antaḥ*), which means between the physical sphere (*golaka*) and its power (*tacchakti*).

If the reading is "O Gopya," it is an address to the Blessed One, meaning that because he is self-luminous, he cannot be illumined by anything else. It is understood that the resonance produced by the initial striking together of the concha and the ear is "song" (*gīta*). //32//
CakBhst_33ab: Through the immersion in the aesthetic flavors (rasa) of existence and non-existence, I am exalted by the grand display of the *tāṇḍava* dance.
CakBhst_33cd: I roar within the path of mantra; what need is there for the contemplation of external objects?

Viv: Through the immersion even in aesthetic flavors such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others—which are the excellences consisting of You—I perform the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the majesty of emotional states (*bhāva*), which is awakened by the various banners and other elements fashioned from the rays of my own light that are scattered about, imitating You. These rays are both mingled and unmixed.
Although my true nature is unshaken by the entry and exit through the curtain of the opening and closing of various states of existence, I nevertheless commence this dance;
as it was said by me in the *Śivarātrivicāravārtika*:
"Constantly manifesting through the sequence of the senses, she is established in hundreds of diverse states..."
Q: Though myself devoid of action, I cause my own rays to dance as dancers, acting as the master of the dance for others.
[From the Śivarātrivicāravārtika of Ramyadeva:
Thus, in the path of mantra (mantrādhvan), which is the abode of resonance (dhvanidhāman) and the state of Paśyantī intent on secret speech;
or rather, in the majesty of the fifth mantra situated in the midst of the sixfold paths of the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakādhva).
"I roar with the joy of the singular density of the Bhairava of Consciousness;
what use have I for the miserable afflictions of conceptualizing external objects?
Thus he manifests the great outpouring of his supreme satisfaction. Or, as another reading has it: "I do not dissolve within, much less here in the external world of becoming."
In that regard, I do not measure nor do I abide; what then to speak of the mundane path of the kalās and so forth, ending with the akala? This is the meaning. //33//

The sky of the contemplation of the state of Śiva, whose form is an unbroken circle, has been fashioned by me as a canopy above Śambhu. (34) Vivaraṇa: It is called a *vitāna* because it extends (*vitanoti*) everything, or because it is extended (*vitanyate*) everywhere. (34)
Having caused the wheel of light to descend through the aperture of the crown from the sky of the heart,
it is held by me before Dhūrjaṭi like a beautiful chowrie.

[This occurs] when the mass of radiant knots has been cast out from the aperture of Brahmā, projected forth by the effort of impelling the staff-like central radiance which shines with the manifestation of the awakened Kuṇḍalinī.
I bear the chowrie, which extends from the sky of the heart and removes the threefold affliction. //35//
O Lord, you are fanned by the breezes from the swans' breath, which have issued forth from the tips of the chambers of your nostrils and spread before you like palm-leaf fans.
Viv: "Issued forth" (visṛtaiḥ) means having entered [the nostrils].
By means of the outspread winds of the *haṃsa*, that is, the vital breaths (*prāṇa-pavana*), which are like fans for the palate and equal to those that lift up. //36//
O noble-minded one, we now hold for you a parasol that is free from all heat and white with the nectar of devotion to you;
it is devoid of the turbidity of attachment to sense objects.
The pure nectar of oneness with you is held as a parasol. //37//

Through the abandonment of the stable of "mine-ness," you are capable of attracting the three worlds; your horse of egoity has been prepared for your mount. Vivṛti: At the commencement of the expedition for victory over the obstructions of existence (*bhava*), when the habitual notions of "I" and "mine" have been destroyed, the egoity (*ahaṅkāra*)—whose essence is full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)—is [your] horse for your supreme transport. (38)
This betel, brilliant with the leaves of the *nāgavallī* creeper—the bliss of the delight of self-awareness—and fragrant with the moon of the throbbing *spanda*, is offered to you.
Regarding "betel" (*tāmbūla*): it is that which has its root in copper (*tāmra*).

Because it delights all, it is like a garden blooming with the joy of one's own awakening; the "serpent" (nāga) is the body, which is a particular kind of wind, and its "creeper" (vallī) is the power of the first emergence of the vital breath— beautiful through the perfection of that [power].
It is perfumed by the camphor-like shimmering of the rising primordial will, because it brings about wonder in both [the subject and the object]. //39//

In the non-dual fire of Śaṅkara, the treasury of all that is auspicious, I offer as an oblation within myself the accumulated fuel of latent impressions arising from the distinction between the enjoyed and the enjoyer. (Vivṛti: I cause the attainment of identity-in-difference in the undivided abode of Śambhu, [offering] the mass of wood consisting of the division between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, and the multitude of latent impressions produced therefrom. //40//
Holding the ladle of *unmanā* with the hands of light and space,
I offer into the fire of the Unborn (*aja*)—

the consumer of the oblation that is the abode of Śiva, which was previously described as established from the beginning of all things and intensified by burning the fuel of the latent impressions of the distinction between subject and object— an offering filled with the fat dripping from both merit and demerit.

I offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)—filled with the clarified butter of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) bound to the qualities of the pleasant and unpleasant fruits that have dissolved by their own inherent force—with my two hands of *samanas* and *unmanā*, whose nature is non-discursive reflection and its subsequent cessation;

these hands are adorned with the five fingers of the subtle faculty of action and its withdrawal. Grasping the *unmanā*-ladle according to the vision that "the Supreme Śiva resides at the end of *unmanā*" due to its movement above those [levels], I offer the full oblation.

Thus, even in a state characterized primarily by dissolution (*saṃkṣaya*), fullness (*pāripūrṇya*) remains entirely undiminished; such is the celebrated principle consisting of identity with the one deity who is both full and emaciated.
And it has been said by me myself in the *Ākulakālikātriṃśikā*:
"Having swallowed the three worlds as a morsel from her own bliss, she devours even her own self, utterly intoxicated."
Q: May she, though satisfied, yet possessing the full majesty of her eternally established and unimpaired sovereignty, protect us in her slender form.
Stained by the rays of the moon of your meditation, may your wish-fulfilling jewel of the mind be mine for the rite of inner contemplation.
[Vivṛti: Inner contemplation (*antarmāna*) is the manifestation of the infinite through internal reflection, preceded by the cessation of external engagement; for that rite...

Rendered helpless by the moonlight of your experience, the mind itself becomes a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) through immersion in you, because like that gem, everything arises by mere volition. //42//

Having placed the consecrated [offering] into the vessel that is the lotus-hand of the Goddess of Liberation, O Blessed One, I offer it as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of my very life-force and all my possessions. Vivṛti:
Their life-force itself, or their entire possession, is the individual nature (*āṇavaṃ svarūpam*).

I announce this— I declare it completely, for I am nourished by the supreme fullness that is eternally accomplished through the elimination of the appearance of the limitations of *māyā*. Having offered that vessel which consists of unbroken attentiveness— the vessel born from the flow of the supreme wave in the hand-water of the Goddess of Consciousness (*saṃviddevī*), whose inclination toward worldly existence has been overturned by the Fortune of Liberation— I offer it.
Thus, having been refined by the refinement of the scriptural tradition of the teachers,

that very [subject] which was introduced with the words "Salutation to the digit of the Sun" (*namaḥ sūryakalā*) and so forth, is now brought to its conclusion through this demonstration of the attainment of the great state of aesthetic fusion (*mahāsāmarasya*), which consists in the movement of the wheel of both sequential and non-sequential processes that sever the various limitations constructed by *māyā*. //43//

Those virtuous ones who desire to cross to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra should resolutely take refuge in the boat of worship through devotion to the Moon-crested Lord. "Should take refuge" means they should attend to it with focused attention.
The raft consisting of the worship of the ultimate nature. //44//
By whatever merit has been acquired through this praise of the feet of Īśānacaraṇa,
may the entire world be liberated from the fault of hatred.
May the world be freed from the violation of the rules for refuting other philosophical systems that arise from the seizure of fixed dogmatic views.

Indeed, for one who possesses the skill of fixed vision, this is the supreme mode of all things, because it consists in the complete penetration of the Supreme Reality, which is the ground of rest for the arising of everything.
As I have stated in the *Kṛtāntatāntiśāntistava*:
"O All-pervading Lord, just as this Māyā has assumed many forms and thus appears manifold, so too is Vidyā dense with infinite divisions; otherwise, how could this [world] exist?"

Q: Some are liberated through the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature; some through discernment; others through the state of being the self of all; and others, through the subsequent vision, are liberated in every respect.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Advayadvādaśikā*:
"If you seek reality by first abandoning unreality, then that very thing is indeed unreality.
If, on the other hand, you seek reality within unreality itself, or even within reality itself—surely such is the nature of reality."
Thus [ends verse 45].

O Supreme Lord, witness of the universe, accept this hymn from me, whose mental states have abandoned both honor and dishonor, who rest my head upon the pedestal of Your pair of feet, whose body is smeared with ashes, and who holds a human skull in hand. [Vivṛti: He is addressed as the witness of the universe (*viśvasākṣin*) or as the one whose form is the universe (*viśvarūpa*).

He whose mental fluctuations are free from honor and dishonor, acceptance and rejection, the manifold and the non-manifold, and the sense of "mine"—or by whom such mental fluctuations have been abandoned;

he who removes (harati) evil (aṃhaḥ), that is, sin; or he whose speech and feet are the ego-maker (ahaṃkṛt); his seat (pīṭha) is the supreme Śiva-nature, which consists of unobstructed knowledge and action.

Therein, he by whom all finite entities— which manifest as limited bodies— have been enveloped and covered by the splendor of the power of awakening (avabodha-bhūti), which is the cause of all prosperity and remains after the burning away of the accumulation of the sheath of the five senses;
and [he by whom] the skull of the minute atom (anu) has been [covered].

He is so described because he holds in one hand a human skull—a potsherd that protects and guards the Brahman which is of the nature of great sovereignty and is undivided—weighed against, that is, measured by the limitedness or finitude characterized by the desire to manifest as the world-marīci. //46//
In the Mahāpāśupata grove, a certain ascetic, having rested, performed supreme praise and meditation upon Śambhu, the Lord of the Wheel of Consciousness (ciccakra).

[This is] in the Mahāpāśupata grove, whose nature is described in the commentary on the word "ash" (*bhasman*) according to the vision [of the scripture]: "In the Goddess’s cremation ground named Karavīra, the web of conceptual constructions regarding the meaning of the scriptures has been cast aside."

The Lord of the Bhairavas and of the bound souls (paśus), whose essence is the sovereign of the unmeasured wheel of consciousness (akalita-cic-cakreśvara-ātman), having rested in that garden— which is the supreme vehicle transcending all—
and having attained a firm establishment through non-duality,
is therefore someone for whom the limitations of fixed designations imagined by the ignorant bound souls do not apply.
In great austerity consisting of immersion in consciousness, Bhava became an ascetic of the Lord of the Wheel of Consciousness— [who is] the ocean of Śiva-consciousness,
whose body is the cognizer, and who is the ground of rest undifferentiated from the various streams of all rivers of consciousness.
*Homage to the ocean of Śiva-consciousness, whose form is the cognizer, and who is the ground of rest undifferentiated from the various streams of all rivers of consciousness.*

By means of such verses, [the author] has offered supreme praise through the state of Śambhu—the source of ultimate bliss—whose nature was described by Rājānaka Utpaladeva, and which consists of the immersion (*samāveśa*) resulting from the unification of all states of being;
thus, by the words *cakranātha* and *cakre*, he reveals his own name, Cakrapāṇi. //47//
I bow to the lineage of gurus, whose physical forms are unseen, who are as vast as the circle of mirages, and whose sole purpose is to bestow grace.

The twice-born Ramyadeva—whose joy and immense enthusiasm were generated by the command bestowed upon him, which was illuminated by the feet of the Goddess Pīṭheśī as they issued from the mouth of the eminent brahmin named Yogānanda; and whose mind was inclined toward dispelling the exhaustion of birth and other sufferings through the teaching of the true secret—composed this commentary on the hymn of offering consisting of inner devotion.
